blocks.content: Design principles are the quiet judges of an LLD interview. You may never say their names out loud, but the interviewer sees clearly whether your classes follow them or fight them.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782974117832-930910673.png

Principles are not rules to recite. They are habits that keep a design clean: each class doing one job, code that is easy to change, and no needless complexity. Applied naturally, they make your design feel professional and senior.
This lesson covers the principles that matter most in LLD, one by one with code, and then the crucial art of knowing when to stop applying them.

blocks.title: How to read this
blocks.content: Understand each principle by its plain meaning and its before and after code. In the interview you rarely name them, you simply design in a way that follows them.
1. Why Principles Matter in LLD
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972226940-909297490.png
blocks.alt: The five SOLID principles in short

blocks.content: Interviewers rarely ask "which principle is this?". Instead they watch whether your design stays clean as it grows and as they add requirements.

["They keep each class focused, so responsibilities do not blur.","They make your design easy to extend when a follow up arrives.","They signal maturity, because clean structure is a senior habit.","They prevent the dreaded giant class that tries to do everything."]
items: They keep each class focused, so responsibilities do not blur.
They make your design easy to extend when a follow up arrives.
They signal maturity, because clean structure is a senior habit.
They prevent the dreaded giant class that tries to do everything.

blocks.content: The SOLID Principles at a Glance
blocks.text: The SOLID Principles at a Glance

blocks.content: SOLID is five principles that together keep object oriented designs clean. Here they are in plain words before we take each in depth.

{"headers":["Letter","Principle","In plain words"],"rows":[["S","Single Responsibility","A class should have one reason to change"],["O","Open Closed","Add new behaviour without editing old code"],["L","Liskov Substitution","A subclass must work wherever its parent does"],["I","Interface Segregation","Keep interfaces small and focused"],["D","Dependency Inversion","Depend on abstractions, not concrete details"]]}
2. Single Responsibility
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972228625-489993662.png
blocks.alt: Split a god class into focused single job classes

blocks.content: A class should have one reason to change. When a class does several unrelated jobs, a change to one job risks breaking the others.
Here is a class doing far too much.

codes.python:
# three jobs in one class: parking, pricing, and printing
class ParkingService:
    def park(self, vehicle): ...
    def calculate_price(self, ticket): ...
    def print_receipt(self, ticket): ...

blocks.content: Now each job gets its own class, so each has a single reason to change.

blocks.title: Why this wins
blocks.content: When pricing rules change, only PricingService changes. Parking and printing are untouched, so a change in one place cannot break the others.
Open Closed
Software should be open for extension but closed for modification. You should be able to add new behaviour by adding code, not by editing code that already works.
A chain of if statements violates this, because every new type forces an edit.
An interface with one class per rule opens it up.
3. Liskov Substitution
A subclass must be usable anywhere its parent is expected, without surprises. If a child breaks the promises of its parent, the inheritance is wrong.
The fix is to model the hierarchy honestly, so a subclass never has to disable what its parent promised. If a Penguin cannot fly, flying does not belong on the Bird base.
Interface Segregation
Keep interfaces small and focused. Do not force a class to implement methods it does not need.
Small interfaces mean a class implements only what it truly does, which keeps the design honest and flexible.
4. Dependency Inversion
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972230326-315681669.png
blocks.alt: High level code depends on an interface, not a concrete class

blocks.content: Depend on abstractions, not on concrete details. High level code should not be nailed to a specific low level class.

blocks.title: Why it helps
blocks.content: Because ParkingLot depends on the Storage interface, you can swap a database for an in memory store, or a fake one for testing, without touching ParkingLot.
DRY: Do Not Repeat Yourself
Avoid copying the same logic in many places. When a rule lives in one spot, you fix it once, not in ten copies.

codes.python:
# repeated logic, easy to get out of sync
car_fee = hours * 10
bike_fee = hours * 10

# one shared source of truth
fee = hours * rate_for(vehicle_type)

blocks.content: DRY is not about removing all repetition blindly. It is about having a single home for each real piece of knowledge in your system.
5. KISS: Keep It Simple
Prefer the plain solution over the clever one. Simple code is easier to read, test, and change, and it is almost always the better choice in an interview.
The best designers are not the ones who add the most. They are the ones who know what to leave out.
6. YAGNI: You Are Not Going to Need It
blocks.text: 6. YAGNI: You Are Not Going to Need It

blocks.content: Do not build features or flexibility nobody asked for. Speculative complexity is a cost you pay now for a benefit that usually never arrives.

blocks.title: YAGNI in action
blocks.text: Do not add a plugin system, caching layer, and five config options to a parking lot the interviewer described in one sentence. Build what was asked, and extend when a real need appears.

blocks.content: 7. Composition Over Inheritance
When choosing how to reuse behaviour, prefer holding another object over extending a class. Composition bends where inheritance breaks.
Deep inheritance chains are fragile: a change high up ripples down and breaks children. Composition keeps pieces independent and swappable.
8. Law of Demeter
Talk only to your immediate friends. A class should not reach deep through a chain of other objects to get what it needs.

codes.python:
# reaching too far, fragile
rate = ticket.get_vehicle().get_owner().get_plan().get_rate()

# ask directly, let each object do its own job
rate = ticket.rate()

blocks.content: Keeping calls shallow reduces coupling, so a change deep in the chain does not ripple back and break distant code.
9. Knowing When to Stop
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972231946-437729760.png
blocks.alt: Balance between under and over engineering

blocks.content: Here is the twist that separates good designers from rule followers: principles have a cost, and applying them everywhere is itself a mistake.
Splitting a tiny class into five, or adding interfaces nobody needs, makes code harder to read, not easier. Apply a principle when it solves a real problem in the design in front of you.
Over engineering and under engineering both make code hard to change. Aim for the middle, guided by the actual needs of the problem.
10. Principles as a Checklist
Near the end of your design, run a quick mental check. It catches most issues in seconds.

["Does any class have more than one clear reason to change?","Would adding a new type force me to edit old code?","Am I repeating the same logic in several places?","Have I added anything nobody actually asked for?","Am I reaching deep through chains of objects?"]
items: Does any class have more than one clear reason to change?
Would adding a new type force me to edit old code?
Am I repeating the same logic in several places?
Have I added anything nobody actually asked for?
Am I reaching deep through chains of objects?

blocks.content: 11. A Worked Example
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972233548-311211042.png
blocks.alt: Pricing built with a strategy behind an interface

blocks.content: Watch several principles work together on a small pricing feature.

blocks.title: The scenario
blocks.text: A parking lot needs hourly, daily, and weekend pricing, with more rules likely later. We want to add rules without editing existing code, and keep pricing separate from parking.

blocks.content: Single Responsibility keeps pricing in its own service, Open Closed lets new rules be new classes, and Dependency Inversion lets any rule be plugged in. Three principles, one clean design.
12. Balancing Principles Against Each Other

Principles sometimes pull in different directions. Aggressive Single Responsibility can create many tiny classes, which can fight readability. Heavy Dependency Inversion adds indirection. Good design is about balance, not maxing out every principle.
["Split responsibilities, but not into meaningless fragments","Depend on abstractions for things that change, not for everything","Remove repetition, but do not hide clear code behind clever reuse"]
items: Split responsibilities, but not into meaningless fragments
Depend on abstractions for things that change, not for everything
Remove repetition, but do not hide clear code behind clever reuse

blocks.content: Principles are servants, not masters. When two of them conflict, choose the design that is easiest to read and change.
13. A Second Example: Notifications
Imagine sending order updates by email, SMS, and push. Applying principles gives a clean design almost automatically.

codes.python:
class Notifier(ABC):                 # dependency inversion
    @abstractmethod
    def send(self, msg): ...


class EmailNotifier(Notifier): ...
class SmsNotifier(Notifier): ...
# adding WhatsApp is a new class, no edits: open closed

blocks.content: Single Responsibility keeps each notifier focused, Open Closed lets new channels be new classes, and depending on the Notifier interface keeps the sender flexible. The principles did the design work for us.
14. Common Mistakes

{"pros":["Give each class one clear job","Depend on abstractions for things that change","Keep the design as simple as it can be","Apply a principle to solve a real need"],"cons":["Cramming many jobs into one class","Hard wiring concrete details everywhere","Adding layers nobody needs","Forcing principles just to look advanced"]}
15. Common Questions
Do I need to name the principles in the interview? - Not necessarily. Applying them well matters more than reciting them, though naming one shows you know what you are doing.
Can I over apply principles? - Absolutely. Splitting everything into tiny classes and interfaces is a real mistake. Apply a principle only where it removes real pain.
Which principle should I focus on first? - Single Responsibility. Most design smells trace back to one class trying to do too much.
Is composition always better than inheritance? - Not always, but it is the safer default. Use inheritance for a true is a relationship, and composition for everything else.
16. Key Takeaways

["Principles keep classes focused and designs easy to change.","SOLID: single responsibility, open closed, Liskov, interface segregation, dependency inversion.","DRY, KISS, and YAGNI keep you from overcomplicating things.","Prefer composition over inheritance, and keep calls shallow.","Apply a principle to solve a real problem, never just to look advanced.","Single Responsibility is the one to reach for first."]
items: Principles keep classes focused and designs easy to change.
SOLID: single responsibility, open closed, Liskov, interface segregation, dependency inversion.
DRY, KISS, and YAGNI keep you from overcomplicating things.
Prefer composition over inheritance, and keep calls shallow.
Apply a principle to solve a real problem, never just to look advanced.
Single Responsibility is the one to reach for first.

blocks.content: Principles keep your classes clean and your design flexible. With that foundation, you are ready to decide when a design pattern genuinely helps, which is the next lesson.
